title: Meeting overrun hourglass
start: A single hourglass about the height of a coffee cup stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its frame is matte graphite metal with four slim turned pillars and chamfered end caps. The bulbs are sandblasted-frosted at the rims and clear in the middle. The upper bulb holds fine ivory sand, and a thin band of acid-lime sand marks one booked hour that is just about to run through. To the right, five ivory paper calendar blocks stand upright on a slim graphite rail, evenly spaced like dominoes waiting their turn, each a thick folded card with a crisp spine and blank front. The falling thread of sand is sharp and fine, and a faint dust of grains rests on the base plate. Everything is orderly, quiet and precisely aligned.
end: The same graphite hourglass now leans forward on its base with the lower bulb overflowing. Pale ivory sand pours in a continuous stream over the base plate and spreads across the tabletop in a soft rippled drift. The lime band has long since run through and lies buried under ivory sand in the lower bulb. The drift has reached the calendar rail: the first two blocks are half buried and leaning, the third is being shoved sideways and creasing at its spine, and the last is caught mid-fall off the table edge with a fine curtain of sand pouring after it. Airborne grains catch the light, a thin haze of dust hangs over the drift, and ripples in the sand run straight back to the hourglass.
apocalypse: A vast miniature desert of pale ivory sand dunes rolls to a hazy horizon, seen from a low, wide viewpoint. Half buried in the nearest dune lies the building-sized fallen frame of a graphite hourglass. One pillar is snapped, and the frosted bulbs are cracked and packed with sand. Around it, the tops of ivory calendar blocks jut from the dunes like weathered monoliths, tilted and broken, their spines bleached and frayed. Wind ripples cross the sand. In the middle distance, a slim graphite sieve conveyor with lime-painted buckets climbs one dune, lifting sand into a rotating frosted drum and dropping small recovered lime tokens into a neat tray. A second graphite rig stakes a taut lime survey line from the drum back to the fallen frame.

title: Quick call that isn't
start: A long brushed graphite day strip about the length of a forearm runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop, with shallow slots along its top edge. Near the left end sits one small ivory paper chip, folded into a tight concertina no wider than a matchbox, its pleats crisp and even. An acid-lime tab on its leading end marks the short call that was booked. Further along the strip, a frosted acrylic lunch block and two ivory focus blocks sit in their slots, evenly spaced with open gaps between them. A graphite end stop caps the right end. Fine paper fibres show along the chip's folds, and light dust sits in the empty slots. The day looks open and uncluttered.
end: The same concertina chip has unfolded along the entire day strip. Its pleats have opened into a long zigzag of ivory paper that fills every slot, rising and sagging as it goes. As it expanded it shoved the frosted lunch block and both focus blocks to the right, where they are piled against the graphite end stop; one focus block has flipped over, and the lunch block is caught mid-fall over the side of the strip. The acid-lime tab is still at the leading edge of the unfolding paper, pressed hard against the pile. Loose pleats bow upward, a torn corner flutters in the air, and creases and paper dust along the strip lead back to the chip's starting slot.
apocalypse: A range of low terraced hills rolls to a hazy horizon, every slope formed from vast weathered pleats of ivory paper, stiffened and greyed at the folds, with scrub growing in the creases. At the far end, the graphite day strip lies as a long broken ridge wall, and the lunch and focus blocks are tumbled boulders the size of houses, cracked and bleached, heaped against the end stop. Wind has frayed the pleat edges into fibrous fringes. On the nearest slope, a slim graphite cutter rig runs on a short rail, slicing the unfolded paper into clean, even segments with a lime wire blade and stacking each section on a lime-edged pallet; the first recovered short block sits squarely in its own restored slot.

title: Out-of-office loop
start: Two brushed graphite mail trays sit facing each other at the left and right of a pale neutral tabletop, about a paperback's length apart, each the size of a paperback. In each tray rests a single ivory envelope, sealed, crisp and blank. Between them runs a short frosted acrylic chute, open at both ends, so either tray can send to the other. On the left tray's rim, a small acid-lime auto-reply toggle is switched on. Behind the right tray, a tiny graphite chair is pushed in with a folded blank ivory card standing on its seat, a sign its owner is away. Light dust lies in the chute. Everything is aligned and quiet.
end: The same two trays are now firing at each other. Envelopes shoot through the frosted chute in both directions, several caught mid-air at its midpoint, colliding and spinning. Each tray is spitting out a new envelope as another lands, and the overflow has built into a dense, sloping pile of ivory envelopes that fills the gap between them and spills off the front of the table. The acid-lime toggle on the left tray is still on, blurred by vibration. The chute has cracked along one side, and the tiny chair behind the right tray has tipped over, its card lying front down. Paper dust hangs in the air, and fresh scuffs show the trays juddering apart.
apocalypse: A narrow gorge runs between two sheer cliff walls, each crowned by a ruined graphite fortress: the two mail trays grown enormous and split open at their rims. Between them, deep drifts of weathered ivory envelopes fill the gorge floor like wind-packed snow, flaps curled, edges softened into fibre. The frosted chute spans the gap high overhead as a cracked, sagging bridge, with envelopes still jammed inside it. Cloud shadows cross the far cliff walls. At the centre of the gorge, a slim graphite tripod rig stands on the drift, lowering a lime cut-off valve into the broken chute on a cable; its lime handwheel is half turned, and on the downstream side the chute is already clear and empty.

title: CC creep
start: At the left of a pale neutral tabletop, one ivory envelope sits in a small brushed graphite launch cradle. From the cradle, a single frosted glass delivery tube about as thick as a pencil runs straight across the table to one graphite mail slot mounted on a short stand at the right. Where the tube meets the cradle it is fitted with an acid-lime collar, the joint where extra copies can be added. The envelope is crisp, blank and flat. Behind the slot, a row of other graphite slots stands unused and capped. Light dust lies along the tube, and the cradle shows fine machining lines. The route is clean and direct.
end: The same frosted tube has split at the acid-lime collar into many branches. New tubes fork again and again, fanning across the tabletop to every capped slot and beyond, some stretching off the table edge. Inside them, the single envelope has divided into dozens of identical copies, frozen mid-travel in every branch, and more copies spill out of open junctions and flutter onto the table. The original slot at the right receives only a crumpled corner. Several tubes have cracked at their joints, with small puffs of paper dust escaping, and the capped slots have popped their caps. The branching pattern traces clearly back to the collar at the cradle.
apocalypse: A wide, pale marsh spreads to a flat horizon, shallow water between grass tussocks reflecting a grey sky. Across it lies a collapsed fan of enormous frosted glass tubes, each as wide as a road, snapped and draped over hummocks, their ends sunk in the mud. Weathered ivory envelopes, sodden and grey, are wedged in broken sections and silted into the shallows. The launch cradle stands as a tilted graphite pier at the left, and the single mail slot rises as a leaning tower far to the right. A slim graphite crawler on long jointed legs steps across the marsh, laying one straight new frosted tube on lime support trestles from the cradle toward the slot, its lime clamps closing each joint.

title: @here broadcast
start: A grid of small brushed graphite desks sits in neat rows across a pale neutral tabletop, each desk the size of a matchbox and holding a small stack of ivory paper, a folded card or a frosted glass tumbler. On the front-left desk stands a small domed desk bell with a graphite base and a sandblasted frosted glass dome, its plunger a tiny acid-lime button. Every other desk carries an identical bell with a plain graphite plunger, unused. The desks are swept clean and aligned edge to edge. Light dust sits on the bell bases, and one paper stack shows a faint ring from a cup. The room is quiet and still.
end: The same grid of desks is shaking. The acid-lime plunger on the front-left bell is pressed down, and every bell across the grid has struck at once: domes are jumping off their bases, and fine lines of lifted dust ripple across the tabletop. Paper stacks slide off the desks and fan into the air, folded cards topple, and a frosted tumbler tips mid-fall, its rim chipping. One bell dome has cracked and is spinning on its edge. The desks have skated out of line, knocked askew in a pattern that spreads outward from the first desk, with the furthest ones pushed nearly to the table edge. Loose sheets hang frozen above the grid.
apocalypse: A broad tidal flat of pale grey mud stretches to a low sea line under an even sky, streaked with shallow channels. Enormous cracked bell domes of sandblasted frosted glass lie scattered across it, each as big as a chapel, tilted and half sunk, their milky surfaces stained. Graphite desks the size of barns lie flattened and thrown outward in rings from a single point, and ivory paper has crusted into the mud around them in weathered sheets. Long wind lines mark the mud between them. A slim graphite rig on wide tracks moves from dome to dome, lowering a lime clamp collar over each one to damp it; the nearest domes already wear lime collars and sit level and silent.

title: Per my last email
start: A single ivory printed sheet rests squarely at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, crisp, with blank grey bars standing in for lines of text. Folded beneath it and showing along its lower edge is a slightly smaller older sheet, and beneath that an even smaller one, each folded in thirds. A brushed graphite clip holds the stack together at the top. An acid-lime tab on the smallest, lowest sheet marks the original message. To the right, a frosted glass tray waits empty, and a graphite letter opener lies angled beside it. Light fibre fuzz shows along the folds. Everything is neat and flat.
end: The same printout has become a tower. Each sheet now holds a smaller copy of the last folded inside it, and the nested sheets have stacked into a tall, telescoping column rising above the graphite clip, each layer slightly offset and leaning. The column bows toward the frosted tray, and its upper layers are sliding off mid-fall, fanning into the air. The acid-lime tab on the original is buried at the base, just visible through a gap. The graphite clip has sprung open and is flying off to the left, and the letter opener has been knocked askew. Dog-eared edges and a haze of paper dust trace the leaning column back to the first sheet.
apocalypse: A range of rounded badland mounds stretches to a pale horizon, each built from collapsed nested paper tunnels: ivory sheets folded inside sheets, weathered grey and fused into crusted layers, with dark openings where tubes have caved in. Rain gullies score the slopes. On the nearest summit, the graphite clip rises as a twisted arch, and the frosted tray lies below it as a cracked basin filled with grit. At the base of the largest mound, a slim graphite boring rig stands on lime-legged footings, its long lime drill string driven straight into the slope; a clean core of neatly stacked sheets slides out onto a cradle beside it, ending in the small original sheet at its tip.

title: Signature attachment snowdrift
start: One ivory envelope lies flat at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, crisp and blank, with a thin frosted acrylic reply card resting on top. Clipped to its lower edge by a small graphite clip are two tiny square image tiles of frosted acrylic, each blank and no bigger than a fingernail. One carries an acid-lime border, the attachment that actually matters. To the left sits an empty graphite letter tray, and to the right a slim folded ivory card. Fine fibres show at the envelope's edges, and light dust rests on the clip. The thread is simple and uncluttered.
end: The same envelope is disappearing under a snowdrift of tiny tiles. With each reply more blank frosted image tiles have clipped on, and now hundreds pour from the envelope's edges in a soft, sloping drift that covers the stacked reply cards and spreads across the tabletop toward the empty letter tray. Some tiles are caught mid-air, flicking up like snowflakes from the top of the pile. The acid-lime bordered tile is half buried near the base, only its lime edge visible. The folded card at the right has been knocked flat. A fine glittering dust of acrylic chips trails back to the graphite clip.
apocalypse: A high snowfield plateau of tiny weathered frosted tiles stretches to a white horizon, wind-packed into long ridged drifts with sharp cornices. From the nearest drift juts the corner of the envelope, now the size of a hangar, its ivory paper bleached, torn and frost-stiffened, the graphite clip still biting its edge like a fallen girder. The letter tray lies half buried in the middle distance, filled to the brim. A slim graphite sifter rig on skids works along the drift's edge, feeding tiles through a lime filter screen; the clutter falls through in a steady stream, and a cleaned strip of the envelope slides out onto a lime tray beside it.

title: Comment pileup
start: An ivory draft page about the size of a postcard stands upright on a slim brushed graphite easel at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its surface lined with faint blank grey bars for text. Pinned into its right margin are three small comment flags, each a tiny ivory paper pennant on a graphite pin. The top flag has an acid-lime pennant, the one comment that matters. At the left sits a small frosted acrylic pin cushion holding a few spare pins, with a graphite pen beside it. Fine fibres show at the page's edge. Everything is spare and clear at a glance.
end: The same draft page is now a pincushion. Hundreds of ivory comment flags on graphite pins have been stuck into it, covering the margins and then the body until the grey bars have vanished. The page bows backward on its easel under the weight, torn around the densest clusters, and more flags are flying through the air toward it from the frosted cushion, which has been emptied and tipped over. Fallen flags lie scattered across the tabletop. The acid-lime pennant is buried deep in the cluster, only a sliver visible. Paper dust and bent pins trace the pile-up back to the margin.
apocalypse: A rolling heathland stretches to a distant ridge under a soft grey sky, and embedded across it lies the draft page, now the size of a valley floor, flattened into the ground and bleached. Thousands of comment flags as tall as trees stand in it, graphite pins leaning, ivory pennants faded and frayed into rags, with heather growing between them. The graphite easel lies toppled along the ridge like a fallen bridge. Through the middle, a slim graphite sweeper rig on wide rollers pulls flags out with lime tongs and stacks them on a lime trailer, leaving one clear lane of bare page that runs straight toward the ridge.

title: Downloads folder landslide
start: A slim graphite chute about the length of a ruler slopes down from the upper left of a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed sides showing fine machining lines and two hex bolts at each bracket. At its lower mouth sits a shallow ivory card tray, crisp-edged and folded at the corners, holding four neat folded paper files squared against its back wall. A fifth file is caught mid-slide in the chute, its crease sharp. To the right, a small frosted acrylic divider block glows softly at its milky edges. The only acid-lime element is a thin lime lip along the tray's front edge, marking where the tray is already nearly full. A faint dust of paper fibres rests along the chute floor. Everything is aligned and quiet.
end: The same graphite chute now carries a dense, continuous stream of identical folded paper files, packed edge to edge and sliding fast. The ivory tray has buckled at one folded corner and tipped forward, and its lime front lip is bent down under the weight of spilling files. Duplicates fan out across the tabletop in a low, spreading slope, overlapping like shingles. The frosted divider block has been shoved sideways and knocked flat, half buried in paper. Several files are frozen airborne above the tray, tumbling end over end, and one hangs off the table edge mid-drop. Creases split, corners dog-ear, and a haze of paper dust hangs over the pile. Every slope of the landslide points straight back up the chute.
apocalypse: A wide miniature valley of layered paper sediment cliffs stretches to a pale horizon, the cliff walls banded with compressed folded files in thin ivory strata. At the foot of the nearest cliff lies the building-sized graphite chute, snapped in two, its brushed metal scoured dull and its bolts rusted into lumps. The ivory tray is a collapsed shell half swallowed by a fan-shaped landslide of weathered duplicates, their edges bleached and frayed. Small scree of loose files trickles down the slopes. In the midground a slim graphite sorting conveyor on long stilt legs reaches into the landslide, its lime sieve belt lifting single files, shaking off duplicates and dropping each unique one into a new, crisp ivory tray set on level ground.

title: Storage full
start: A frosted acrylic storage canister about the height of a pint glass stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, capped top and bottom with chamfered matte graphite rings held by six small screws. Through its milky walls, tightly rolled ivory paper files are faintly visible, packed to just below the rim. A plain graphite dial on the lid shows tick marks, and its slim acid-lime needle rests almost at the top of the arc. To the left, a small graphite funnel feeds one more rolled file toward the lid opening. To the right, two empty frosted glass jars wait unused. Fine scuffs mark the graphite rings and a light film of paper dust rings the base. The scene is still and orderly.
end: The same canister has split along a vertical seam, the frosted acrylic cracked open in a jagged line from lid to base. The graphite lid ring has popped free and hangs tilted, its screws sheared, and the lime needle is bent hard past the end of the dial. Rolled ivory files burst outward from the seam, unrolling mid-air in long curling ribbons that spray across the tabletop. The funnel on the left has toppled, still pushing a file in. One unrolled sheet has draped over the two empty frosted jars on the right, which sit untouched. Shards of acrylic and loose screws are frozen mid-bounce, and a cloud of paper fibre hangs over the split. Every ribbon traces back to the seam.
apocalypse: A broad flooded basin stretches to a low horizon, its shallow still water clouded with dissolved paper pulp and scattered with floating ivory sheets. At the centre, the tower-sized frosted acrylic canister lies collapsed on its side, split open, its graphite rings pitted and dark with water stains, the plain dial cracked. Unrolled files lie in soggy mats along the waterline, bleached and swollen. The two frosted jars stand as tall, weathered cisterns at the basin edge, still empty. In the midground a slim graphite pipeline on thin trestles crosses the water, its lime pump housing drawing pulp-laden water from the ruin and filling the first of the two old cisterns, a clear line of flow rising inside its frosted wall.

title: #REF chain collapse
start: A row of six frosted acrylic cell blocks, each the size of a matchbox, stands on a pale neutral tabletop in a gentle curve from left to right. Between each pair runs a slim brushed graphite linkage rod, pinned to the blocks with small ball joints, so that each block depends on the one before it. The first rod, at the far left, has an acid-lime pull tab on its pin, the single link that holds the chain in place. Small graphite marbles rest in shallow cups on top of each block. Behind the row, an ivory card lies folded and square. Faint machining rings show on the joints, and fine dust sits around the bases. Every rod is taut and level.
end: The same row is mid-collapse. The lime pull tab has been drawn out, and the first rod has dropped free, its end frozen just above the tabletop. The first block has tipped backward, yanking the next rod, and the failure is running down the curve: each block is tilting further than the last, rods swinging loose, ball joints popping. Graphite marbles have leapt from their cups and are frozen mid-air in a scattered arc, a few already bouncing across the table. The last block is caught mid-fall over the edge. The folded ivory card behind has been knocked open. A trail of scuffs and marble tracks leads back along the curve to the empty pin hole where the lime tab sat.
apocalypse: A wide terraced hillside of weathered ivory paper steps down toward a hazy horizon, each terrace edge crumbling. Across it lie the giant ruins of the linkage chain: building-sized frosted cell blocks toppled on different terraces, their sursurfaces cracked and clouded, and long graphite rods lying bent between them or jutting from the slope, their ball joints split. Heavy graphite marbles have rolled down the terraces and rest in gullies, half sunk in paper scree. At the top of the slope, a slim graphite linkage rig on jointed stilt legs stands astride the first fallen block, its lime pin driver seating a fresh rod into a restored joint, reconnecting the first two blocks as a straight, taut link.

title: Duplicate CRM contacts
start: A small graphite card file about the size of a shoebox sits on a pale neutral tabletop, with two shallow drawers, brushed fronts, chamfered edges and slim pull handles. The top drawer is open, showing a neat row of ivory contact cards standing upright, each with a crisp top edge and a blank front, separated by unmarked frosted acrylic tab dividers. One card near the front has an acid-lime corner, marking a contact that has just been duplicated: its identical twin stands directly behind it. To the right, a small graphite stamp and an ivory card stack sit squared. Fine fibres show at the card edges and dust gathers in the drawer runners. Everything is otherwise aligned.
end: The same card file is bursting. Starting from the lime-cornered card, every card has copied itself again and again: the top drawer is jammed wide open with cards packed so tight they bow and fan upward, and the lower drawer has been forced out of its runners and hangs tilted. Cards spray out of both drawers in thick sheaves, frozen mid-air in overlapping arcs, and pile across the tabletop in slumping stacks of identical copies. Frosted tab dividers have popped out and lie scattered. The graphite stamp on the right has been knocked over. A haze of paper dust hangs above the file, and every drift of cards slopes back toward the lime corner.
apocalypse: A wide pale tundra of wind-packed card drifts stretches to a flat, cold horizon, the surface rippled into long sastrugi ridges made of thousands of identical ivory contact cards, their edges frayed and bleached. In the foreground, the building-sized graphite card file lies on its back, both drawers torn open and packed solid with compressed cards, its brushed front scoured dull and its handles snapped. Frosted tab dividers stand upright in the drifts like weathered markers. In the midground, a slim graphite dedupe press on caterpillar tracks works along one ridge, its lime compaction plate pressing matching cards together and releasing one single, crisp card at a time onto a short, neat stack on a graphite pallet.

title: Adapter stack
start: A slim graphite laptop sits open at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed shell showing fine machining lines and a single small port on its left side. Plugged into that port is one compact graphite adapter block about the size of a matchbox, chamfered at its edges, with a short frosted acrylic cable leading to a small monitor stand made of an ivory card box. To the left, a graphite tray holds a projector puck and a card reader, both unconnected. The adapter's only acid-lime part is its ringed plug collar, marking the laptop's one available port. Dust sits in the tray corners and faint scuffs mark the laptop's edge. The setup is simple and neat.
end: The same single port is now holding up a teetering tower of adapters: graphite blocks plugged into graphite blocks, dongles plugged sideways into dongles, stacked in a leaning column that rises above the laptop lid and bends out over the table. The lime plug collar at the base is strained and cracking. Frosted cables hang from every level, dragging the projector puck and card reader off their tray. The tower is caught mid-lean, its top blocks frozen as they tip and fall, one block bouncing off the laptop keyboard. The ivory card stand has been knocked over. Fine plastic dust and a loose screw hang in the air, all falling away from the port.
apocalypse: A rugged boulder field spreads across a wide butte toward a hazy horizon, the boulders made of giant weathered graphite adapter blocks, chipped, rusted and piled in toppled towers that have fallen outward like collapsed chimneys. Long bleached acrylic cables lie across the rubble like dried roots. At the centre of the field, the building-sized laptop lies open and tilted, its single port packed with the snapped base of the old tower, the ivory card stand crumpled beside it. In the midground, a slim graphite crane on a narrow tracked base has cleared a patch of flat ground and is lowering one clean, compact lime hub block into place beside the laptop, a single neat cable ready to connect.

title: Retry storm
start: A slim graphite chute about the length of a ruler slopes from a small graphite launcher on the left of a pale neutral tabletop down to a frosted acrylic receiving tray on the right. The launcher is a compact brushed block with a spring plunger and chamfered edges. One small ivory card message cube is mid-way down the chute, sliding smoothly. The receiving tray has a small hinged acknowledgement flap, and its acid-lime flag is folded down, waiting to pop up when the message lands. Beside the tray, a small stack of ivory cards sits squared. Fine machining marks show on the chute sides and a faint dust lies along its floor. The path is clear and quiet.
end: The same receiving tray has not answered: its lime flag is still folded down. Behind it, the launcher has fired again and again, and now the chute is packed end to end with ivory message cubes that have jammed into a solid column, bulging over the chute walls. More cubes are frozen mid-launch above the plunger, colliding with each other. Cubes spill over the chute sides and pile across the tabletop, burying the stack of cards beside the tray. The chute is bending under the weight, a bracket bolt popping loose. A spray of paper dust and crushed cube fragments hangs in the air, and every heap traces back up the chute to the launcher.
apocalypse: A wide, shallow crater of pale paper earth stretches toward a hazy rim horizon, its floor heaped with countless weathered ivory message cubes, cracked and faded, piled into scree slopes against a giant graphite launcher that lies toppled on its side at the crater's centre, its plunger rusted mid-stroke. The long chute projects out of the heap like a broken ramp, crushed at the middle. The frosted receiving tray stands at the crater edge as a clouded, cracked basin, its hinged flap rusted shut. In the midground, a slim graphite valve rig on four thin legs sits astride the chute's intact end, its lime metering valve letting through one single cube at a spaced interval toward the tray.

title: Make the logo bigger
start: A flat ivory layout board about the size of a placemat lies centred on a pale neutral tabletop, its thick card edges crisp and faintly fibrous. Seated on it in a neat grid are six blocks: a long ivory headline bar across the top, two frosted acrylic image tiles with milky edges in the middle, and three narrow ivory text slabs along the bottom. In the upper left corner sits a small matte graphite mark block the size of a sugar cube, its chamfered edges catching light. A slim acid-lime alignment ruler runs along the board's left margin, keeping every block square. A few fine paper fibres and a single scuff mark on the board surface are the only disorder. Everything is balanced, calm and evenly spaced.
end: The same layout board, but the graphite mark block has swollen in visible steps to the size of a brick, with faint seams showing each enlargement like nested shells. It has shoved the headline bar sideways off the top edge, where it hangs mid-fall at an angle. Both frosted image tiles are pushed to the right margin, one tipping over the edge and the other cracked at a corner. The three text slabs are crushed into a creased ivory pile against the lower right corner. The acid-lime alignment ruler has been knocked askew and is sliding off the left edge. Paper dust and small acrylic chips hang in the air, all scattered outward from the graphite block, tracing the push back to its swollen corner.
apocalypse: A wide, low view across an overgrown plain of pale dry grass and ivory paper scraps stretching to a soft horizon. Dominating the midground is the enormous graphite mark block, now the size of a warehouse, weathered and pitted, its chamfered edges chipped and streaked with dust. Around its base, flattened ivory layout slabs lie half sunk in the ground like fallen paving, their surfaces cracked and softened by rain. A frosted acrylic image tile juts from the grass at an angle, its milky front clouded and chipped. In the foreground, a slim graphite gantry crane on four spindly legs is lowering a large square acid-lime grid frame over one of the flattened slabs, measuring it back to its original proportion. Seed heads and fine dust drift through the air.

title: Ad size explosion
start: A small matte graphite easel, about the height of a wine bottle, stands in the centre of a pale neutral tabletop with slim legs and a knurled height knob. On it rests one finished ad frame: a crisp ivory card panel inside a thin brushed graphite border, with blank blocks for image and headline. A single acid-lime button shape sits in the lower right corner of the ad, the one element that has just been changed. Beside the easel lie a graphite craft knife and a frosted acrylic cutting ruler, both perfectly aligned. Light dust rests on the table. The scene is calm, with one small edit waiting to be applied.
end: The same graphite easel is now surrounded by dozens of ad frames in every proportion, tall skinny banners, wide strips, tiny squares and oversized panels, fanning outward across the tabletop and stacked against each other. Each is a copy of the original, and each has its acid-lime button placed slightly differently, some cut in half by the border, some floating. The easel is leaning under the weight of frames propped against it. A tall banner is toppling over at the back, and a small square is frozen mid-slide off the table's edge. Card offcuts and graphite border shavings are scattered around the craft knife, and the fan radiates outward from the easel.
apocalypse: A terraced quarry cut into pale ivory card stone descends in wide steps toward a hazy basin, seen from a high edge. Each terrace is crowded with enormous ad frames in mismatched proportions, leaning in rows, cracked, bleached and chipped at their graphite borders. At the bottom of the quarry the original easel stands as a toppled ruin, legs snapped and splayed like a fallen tower. Offcuts form drifts along the terrace walls. On the upper terrace, a slim graphite gantry on straight rails holds an acid-lime cutting frame over a single oversized panel, trimming it down to a clean proportion. A neat row of three already-resized frames stands beside the gantry.

title: Everything is urgent
start: A neat row of five ivory task cards, each the size of a coaster with crisp edges and blank fronts, stands upright in slim graphite card holders along a pale neutral tabletop. Only the middle card carries a small flag: a thin graphite pin with a triangular acid-lime pennant, clearly marking the one task that matters today. The other cards are plain and evenly spaced. At the back, a frosted acrylic pin box holds a few spare graphite pins. The card fibres show fine grain and a faint crease on one corner. The scene is quiet, with a single clear priority.
end: The same row of task cards is now buried under flags. Graphite pins with ivory pennants are stuck into every card, then into the pennants themselves, forming bristling thickets that bend the cards backward in their holders. The original acid-lime pennant is barely visible deep inside the middle thicket. The frosted pin box has been emptied and knocked on its side. Two cards have collapsed under the weight and are frozen mid-fall, shedding pins across the tabletop. Loose pennants float down through the air. Nothing of the actual task fronts can be seen anymore, and the heaviest pile sits exactly where the first flag was.
apocalypse: A windswept tundra of pale gravel and ivory card fragments stretches to a flat horizon, bristling with countless weathered flags. Enormous graphite pins stand at every angle like dead trees, their faded ivory pennants torn, bleached and flapping in the wind. Toppled task cards the size of barns lie half buried among them, their fronts lost under the flag thickets. In the midground, a long slim graphite sorting rack on crawler legs moves slowly across the ground, plucking pins from the gravel with fine arms. It has raised only three flags onto its top rail, and one of them bears an acid-lime pennant standing clearly above the rest.

title: Context switching
start: A small round matte graphite desk, about the size of a dinner plate, sits on a turntable base at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Arranged around it in a neat circle are six shallow ivory card task trays, each holding a single blank work sheet. A slim graphite writing arm on the desk points at one tray. The acid-lime element is a small indicator notch on the desk's rim showing the current facing direction. The trays are evenly spaced like hours on a dial. Fine paper fibres and a faint circular scuff on the tabletop show where the desk turns. Everything is still and ordered.
end: The same graphite desk is spinning fast on its turntable, motion-blurred at its edges, with the acid-lime notch smeared into a faint streak. Every one of the six ivory trays now holds a half-finished sheet: one partly folded, one half torn, one with a graphite pencil line stopping mid-stroke. The writing arm has flung loose sheets outward, frozen in a spiral of airborne paper around the desk. Two trays have been knocked askew and one has tipped over, spilling its work. Dust and paper shreds hang in a ring above the table. The spiral of debris leads back to the spinning desk.
apocalypse: A windswept hilltop of pale scrub and ivory paper drifts overlooks a hazy valley. Crowning the hill is the enormous graphite desk, seized on its cracked turntable, tilted at an angle and streaked with dust. Around it in a wide, broken ring lie six ruined ivory trays the size of courtyards, each filled with weathered half-finished sheets now bleached and matted into the ground. A spiral of old paper debris still curls outward across the hillside. Beside the desk's base, a slim graphite brake rig has clamped an acid-lime caliper onto the turntable edge, holding the desk still and facing one single tray.

title: Kitchen mug tower
start: A small ivory office-kitchen sink, about the size of a lunchbox, is set into a pale neutral counter, its basin smooth with a brushed graphite tap and a round graphite drain. In the basin rests one unwashed matte ivory mug with a faint brown coffee ring inside and a tiny chip on its rim. The acid-lime element is this mug's handle, the one clue to whose mug it is. Beside the sink stands an empty frosted acrylic drying rack with a folded ivory cloth hung over its edge, and a sponge sits dry on the drain board. Fine water spots and light dust mark the counter. Everything is tidy apart from the one mug left behind.
end: The same sink is now crowned by a tall leaning tower of mugs stacked rim on rim on the first one, rising well above the graphite tap and curving out over the counter. Ivory, graphite and frosted glass mugs are wedged together at uneven angles, the lower ones cracked under the weight. The top of the tower is frozen mid-topple: one mug is falling toward the floor, another is bouncing off the counter and a third has just shattered beside the rack. The acid-lime handle of the first mug is just visible at the base. Drops of stale coffee spray outward from the falling mugs, and the lean traces straight back to the sink.
apocalypse: A pale shoreline made of broken ceramic shards runs along a quiet grey sea toward a misty horizon. In the midground, the enormous toppled mug tower lies across the beach like a fallen stone column, its mugs cracked, stained and chipped, the outer end sliding into the shallows. Behind it, the ruined sink juts from the shards at an angle, its graphite tap bent and streaked with mineral deposits. Small waves wash shards along the tide line, and old coffee stains mark the rims. In the foreground, a slim graphite sorting rig on tall jointed legs picks through the shard beach with long tweezer arms, setting only the few intact mugs in a neat row on an acid-lime drying rack.

title: Mailroom parcel pile
start: A single ivory card parcel about the size of a paperback sits on a long matte graphite mailroom counter at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. The box has crisp folded corners, a faint fibre texture and a blank label squared on its lid, and it is tied with a thin acid-lime strap that marks it as the first delivery still waiting to be sorted. Behind it, a wall of graphite pigeonholes with chamfered edges stands empty in tidy rows. To the left, a small frosted acrylic intake chute slopes down to the counter, its milky lip catching soft light. To the right, a brushed graphite trolley waits with its wheels aligned. A little paper dust sits in the counter seams. Everything is quiet, squared and ready.
end: The same mailroom counter is now buried. Ivory card parcels pour out of the frosted acrylic chute on the left in a steady frozen stream, tumbling end over end in mid-air. They have stacked into a leaning pile that fills the counter and has spilled onto the trolley, whose wheels are skewed sideways under the load. The graphite pigeonholes behind are jammed with boxes wedged in at angles, and the side panels of the pigeonhole wall bow outward, fasteners popping loose. The first parcel with its acid-lime strap is visible at the bottom of the pile, crushed flat. Corners are dented, blank labels peel, and a haze of card dust and loose packing scraps hangs over the pile, every trail leading back to the chute.
apocalypse: A long miniature valley seen from a high ridge, its floor filled by a vast landslide of weathered ivory parcels, some the size of houses, crushed into terraced sediment layers along the valley walls. At the head of the valley, the giant frosted acrylic intake chute juts from a cliff, cracked and clouded, still aimed downhill. Snapped graphite pigeonhole frames poke from the slope like the ribs of a collapsed building. The boxes are bleached, softened at the corners and seamed with fine dust. In the foreground, a slim graphite gantry on splayed legs straddles the rubble, feeding recovered parcels onto an acid-lime sorting chute that splits into three neat lanes, each lane ending in a short tidy row of boxes on the clean valley floor below. Mist fills the distance.

title: Shredder jam
start: A desktop paper shredder about the size of a shoebox sits centre frame on a pale neutral tabletop. Its head is matte graphite with chamfered corners and a row of hex fasteners, and it rests on a frosted acrylic bin whose milky walls show a small soft pile of ivory strips inside. A single ivory sheet is half fed into the slot, slightly skewed. The feed slot is lined with a thin acid-lime guide lip, the one part meant to keep sheets straight. To the left, a neat short stack of sheets waits on a graphite tray, and to the right a spare bin lid leans against the machine. Fine paper fibres cling to the slot edges. The scene is still and orderly, apart from the skewed page.
end: The same graphite shredder is now jammed and bulging. The skewed sheet has crumpled into the slot and bent the acid-lime guide lip upward. Behind it, the waiting stack has been fed in too fast and is caught half inside, pleated like a fan. Ivory paper strips burst out of every seam, from the gap between head and bin, from the vent slots and from under the base, frozen mid-spray in curling fountains. The frosted acrylic bin is overfull, its walls pushed apart, and strips spill across the tabletop in a wide fan to the right, slipping off the table edge. The graphite tray on the left has tipped and slid toward the machine. Fibre dust hangs in the air, every trajectory leading back to the jammed slot.
apocalypse: A broad windswept plain under a low grey sky is covered in rolling drifts of weathered ivory paper strips that ripple like tundra grass toward a far horizon. Near the centre rises the building-sized graphite shredder ruin, split open along its seams, its cutting head exposed and scaled with dull grit, bleached strips still caught in the fallen blades. Its frosted acrylic bin lies cracked nearby, clouded and filled with drift. The strips have matted into layers, wind-combed in one direction. In the foreground, a slim graphite tracked compactor with an acid-lime press plate is working across one drift, leaving behind a tidy row of dense, square ivory bales bound with thin graphite bands and a clean strip of bare ground in its wake.

title: Sticky-note wall collapse
start: A freestanding frosted acrylic wall panel about the height of a laptop screen stands upright at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, held by two brushed graphite feet with chamfered fasteners. On it, a dozen small square ivory paper notes sit in three neat rows, each with a gentle curl at its lower edge and a blank front. One note in the top row is acid-lime, the priority everyone agreed on. A slim graphite rail along the bottom holds a tidy pad of fresh notes and a graphite marker lying flat. In front, the tabletop is bare. Fine fibres show along the note edges, and a few corners are very slightly lifting away from the acrylic.
end: The same frosted acrylic panel is now shingled edge to edge with ivory notes layered on notes, many deep, the mass thick and heavy. Under that weight the whole skin has peeled away from the top of the panel and is curling forward in one great sheet, caught mid-fall with its lower edge still stuck. Hundreds of loose notes flutter free from the curl, spinning in the air and settling in a spreading drift across the tabletop. The acid-lime priority note has slid under the pile and shows only one corner. The graphite rail has bent downward, the fresh pad has fanned open, and one graphite foot has lifted off the table as the panel tips forward. Paper dust hangs in the light.
apocalypse: A steep mountain cirque seen from below, where a long scree slope of weathered ivory notes pours down from a broken ridge line, the squares compacted into flaky layers and scattered boulders of fused paper. Rising from the slope is the snapped, building-sized frosted acrylic wall panel, clouded and cracked, leaning against the rock with one graphite foot jutting into the air. Wind has curled the loose notes into small drifts, their edges bleached and frayed. At the base of the slope, a slim graphite climbing rail runs straight up the fallen panel, and a small carriage with acid-lime suction pads is lifting notes one at a time from the scree and pressing them back onto the panel in three clean rows, the restored patch bright against the ruin.

title: Survey fatigue
start: A shallow brushed graphite inbox tray palm-sized sits front left on a pale neutral tabletop, holding a single ivory survey card printed with a grid of small blank tick boxes and one acid-lime corner tab that marks it as answered. To the right stands a slim frosted acrylic drop box with a milky slot on top, empty and glowing softly. A graphite paperclip rests on the tray rim. Behind, a second empty tray waits on a short graphite riser. The card has crisp edges and a faint fibre grain, and a thin line of dust sits along the tray's machined lip. One more survey card is just visible sliding in from the back edge of the frame.
end: The same graphite inbox tray is overwhelmed. Ivory survey cards pour in from the back edge in a frozen cascade, fanning through the air and heaping over both trays until the riser has buckled and tipped forward. The frosted acrylic drop box is stuffed so full that cards jut from its slot and bulge its thin walls. Nearly every card is blank, its tick boxes untouched. The single answered card with the acid-lime tab is sinking into the pile, only its corner still showing. Cards slide off the table edge in a sheet, and a haze of dust rises where they land. The paperclip has been flicked into the air, and every card trail points back to the source edge.
apocalypse: A broad glacier of compacted ivory survey cards winds down a mountain valley toward a hazy lowland, its surface split by crevasses that expose layered strata of blank cards. Locked into the pale mass are the building-sized ruins of the frosted acrylic drop box, cracked and clouded, and the tilted graphite trays, one lip snapped off. Wind has sculpted the card surface into sharp ridges with bleached, frayed edges. In the foreground, a slim graphite sled rig on long skids works slowly across the glacier with a thin probing arm, plucking out the rare answered cards, recognisable by their marked tick boxes, and filing them upright into an acid-lime collecting rack on its back, which is already half full.

title: Broken link
start: A chain of five ivory card page tiles, each about the size of a playing card with crisp edges and blank fronts, runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop on small graphite stands. The tiles are joined by short brushed graphite links with machined pins, except the link between the third and fourth tile, which is acid-lime and already hairline cracked. A small frosted acrylic bead, the size of a pea, rolls along a narrow groove through the chain from left to right, and a second bead waits at the start. The tiles are evenly spaced and level. A faint line of dust marks the groove. Everything is calm, with the one weak link easy to find.
end: The same chain of ivory page tiles has split at the acid-lime link, which has snapped in two, its halves swinging downward on their pins. The third and fourth tiles have tilted away from each other, opening a gap. Frosted acrylic beads keep arriving along the groove from the left and pour straight off the broken end, frozen in a falling column into the gap and scattering across the tabletop below. A pile of beads has built up beneath the break and has started pushing the fourth tile's stand sideways. The last two tiles, still linked, sit stranded and empty. Dust and tiny acrylic chips spray outward, and the bead trail traces cleanly back to the first tile.
apocalypse: A vast chasm splits a high rocky plateau, its walls layered in pale sediment and dropping into deep blue haze. Across it once ran a monorail of giant ivory page tiles on graphite pylons; now the line ends in a jagged break on both sides, the tile sections weathered, bleached and cracked, and the old snapped link hanging in pieces. Far below, a drift of clouded frosted acrylic beads the size of boulders fills the chasm floor. The remaining tiles stretch away along the plateau toward the horizon. At the break, a slim graphite cantilever crane anchored on the near edge is lowering a single acid-lime rail section into the gap on taut cables, its ends only a short drop from the pylons.

title: Friday hotfix
start: A thick brushed graphite plate about the size of a coaster lies flat on a pale neutral tabletop, a machined part with chamfered edges and fine milling marks. A thin crack runs across it. Over the crack sits a small ivory card patch, taped down at its corners, and at its centre a single acid-lime rivet pins the patch in place. To the right, a tidy row of three more ivory patches and a small graphite driver tool wait on a frosted acrylic tray. To the left sits a closed ivory card lunch box, packed and ready for the weekend. Fine grit sits in the crack. Everything else is neat, and the fix looks almost good enough.
end: The same graphite plate is now split wide, the crack branching in several directions. Patch after patch has been layered over it in a hurry, ivory card squares overlapping at odd angles, some bolted, some taped, some already tearing. Small graphite bolts are frozen mid-air as the patches lift and pop them loose. The original acid-lime rivet has sheared and sits at the bottom of the widening crack. The frosted acrylic tray is empty and knocked sideways, and the driver tool has rolled away. The plate has lifted at one edge, breaking in two, and graphite fragments and card scraps spray outward, all tracing back to the first crack. The closed lunch box sits untouched on the left.
apocalypse: A vast dry lakebed of pale clay cracked into deep polygons stretches to a low horizon, with one enormous fissure running straight across it. The building-sized graphite plate lies split along that fissure, its halves tilted, its surface crusted with layers of weathered ivory card patches many deep, curled, bleached and peeling like old paint, with loose bolts scattered in the clay. Dust devils rise in the distance. In the midground, a slim graphite rig on four splayed legs is lowering a single long acid-lime brace across the fissure and bolting it to both halves, while a small graphite gauge with a plain dial with tick marks, mounted beside it, shows the gap closing.
